title: Motivate judgements on selected literary texts

lessons.title: Forming a judgement
lessons.html:
What it means to motivate a judgement

To motivate a judgement means to state a clear opinion about a literary text and support it with reasons and evidence so that others can follow and assess your thinking. "I liked this story" is a preference. "This story is effective because its spare, repetitive language mirrors the monotony of the farm worker's life, as seen in..." is a motivated judgement.

Types of judgement

  • Aesthetic: about the quality of the writing and its artistry.
  • Interpretive: about what the text means.
  • Ethical or social: about the values the text promotes or challenges, and how it represents people and society.
  • Relevance: about the text's significance for a particular audience today.

Developing your judgement

  1. Read the text more than once.
  2. Note your first response honestly, then ask why you responded that way.
  3. Gather evidence: quotations, events, images, structural features.
  4. Consider the writer's purpose, audience and context.
  5. Test your view: what would someone who disagrees say? Is your evidence strong enough?
  6. Refine your judgement into a clear thesis statement.

Example thesis statements

  • "In this poem about a drought-stricken farm, the poet's use of silence and empty space on the page is more powerful than any description of suffering could be."
  • "The play's portrayal of the farm owner is one-dimensional, which weakens its message about reconciliation."

A good thesis is specific, arguable and can be supported with evidence from the text.

lessons.title: Supporting and presenting a judgement
lessons.html:
Building the argument

Every claim needs support. Use a clear structure for each point:

  1. Claim: what you are arguing.
  2. Evidence: a short quotation or specific reference to the text.
  3. Analysis: how the evidence supports the claim, focusing on technique and effect.
  4. Link: how this point connects to your overall judgement.

Kinds of evidence

  • Direct quotation, kept short and accurate.
  • Reference to events, dialogue or a character's actions.
  • Patterns: repeated images, symbols, words.
  • Structural features: the order of events, a surprise ending, a shift in narrator.
  • Context: historical or biographical information, used to illuminate, not replace, analysis of the text.
  • Critical opinions: views of published critics, acknowledged as such.

Avoiding weak arguments

WeaknessExampleFix
Unsupported claim"The ending is bad."Explain why with evidence.
Plot summary instead of analysisRetelling the storyFocus on how and why.
Over-generalising"All farm novels are sad."Limit claims to the text discussed.
Judging the author, not the text"The writer is a bad person."Discuss the writing and its effects.

Presenting orally

In a discussion or presentation, state your judgement early, give two or three well-supported reasons, read short quotations clearly, and finish by summarising. Speak to the audience, not to your notes.

lessons.title: Responding to other judgements
lessons.html:
Engaging with different views

Readers bring different experiences to a text. A farm worker, a landowner and a student in the city may respond very differently to the same story about land. These differences can enrich understanding.

Respectful debate

  • Listen fully to another reader's judgement before responding.
  • Identify their claim and their evidence.
  • Acknowledge strong points: "You make a good point about the symbolism of the windmill."
  • Respond with evidence, not emotion: "However, in the final chapter..."
  • Be willing to adjust your view if their argument is stronger.

Evaluating critics' judgements

When reading a review or critical essay, ask: What is the critic's thesis? What evidence do they use? Do they consider the text's context? Do they acknowledge other views? Do you agree, and why?

Reflecting on your own judgement

After discussion, write a short reflection: Has your judgement changed? What persuaded you? What would you look for in your next reading? This reflective habit strengthens critical thinking.

Application at work

Motivating judgements is a core business skill. Recommending a supplier, defending a promotion budget, or responding to a customer's complaint all require a clear position supported by evidence, presented respectfully, with openness to other views.

Key points

  • A motivated judgement is a clear opinion supported by reasons and evidence.
  • Write a specific, arguable thesis.
  • Use claim, evidence, analysis and link for each point.
  • Avoid unsupported claims, plot summary and over-generalising.
  • Engage respectfully with other views and be willing to refine your own.

The ending is abrupt, as the final line cuts off mid-sentence, leaving the conflict unresolved.
